text: Lynn Conway was born in Mount Vernon, New York, in 1938. Raised in Hartsdale and White Plains, she experienced gender dysphoria and attempted a gender transition in her youth, eventually detransitioning after facing social and medical challenges. She earned a B.S. and M.S.E.E. from Columbia University and joined IBM in 1964, where she contributed to the design of advanced supercomputers and invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling. In 1968, IBM fired her after she revealed her intention to transition. After reentering the field as a contract programmer, she joined Xerox PARC in 1973, where she co-authored *Introduction to VLSI Systems* with Carver Mead, revolutionizing chip design. She founded the MOSIS system, enabling rapid prototyping and short-run fabrication of chips, which became foundational to the VLSI industry. Conway later joined DARPA and the University of Michigan, where she specialized in visual communications and control systems. She coined the term "Conway effect" to describe how marginalized groups are overlooked in historical accounts of innovation. A prominent transgender rights activist, she advocated for equal opportunities and against the pathologization of transgender people. She was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2023 and received numerous awards, including the IEEE/RSE James Clerk Maxwell Medal and a Lifetime Achievement Award from IBM. Conway died in 2024 at age 86.
